column2: Take three kinds of auditor qualification seriously:
1. The company set aside less than needed for tax or doubtful debts. 2. Related companies haven’t paid their debts for a long time. 3. The auditor doubts the company can keep going.
A qualification that repeats for several years and gets bigger means managers don’t intend to fix it.
Also read the “other legal responsibilities” section of the auditor’s report.
If a mechanic tells you three years in a row “the brake pads need changing” and you don’t change them, the problem isn’t the pads; it’s the driver.
Three auditor qualifications that matter
Read each note with one question:
Inventory and money owed by customers: are they growing faster than sales? Are the debts getting older?
Provisions: did the company make profit by reversing earlier provisions? Fixed assets: did it count machines as lasting longer so costs look smaller?
The dollar and related companies: big profit from a change in the dollar rate, or cheap sales to group companies?
Like checking a shop’s accounts: how old the credit sales are, how much stock is gathering dust, and whether the owner sells cheaply to relatives.
Inflation makes profit look bigger than it is in two ways.
1. Goods made cheaply are sold at high prices; but the company has to fill the warehouse again at the new price, so this profit doesn’t become free money.
2. Wear and tear on machines is counted at old prices. The note on asset insurance shows what replacing them would cost today.
If you sell rice this year for 150 a kilo that you bought last year for 100, you made 50 profit; but to refill the store you have to pay 150, and that profit is no longer in your pocket.
This ratio says how much of profit hasn’t turned into cash yet: (profit − cash from the company’s work) ÷ assets.
Negative or small means cash came in equal to or above profit; that’s good.
In Iran with high inflation this number is usually a little positive. If it is above about 10% two years in a row and higher than peers, look for the reason.
If your yearly profit is 1,000 but only 200 of it has reached your account, most of it is still on paper.
How much of profit hasn’t become money yet?
These are signs of dressing up profit:
Profit goes up two years in a row but cash doesn’t; or at year-end, when the year’s target wasn’t met, a big non-operating gain suddenly appears.
Provisions are reversed in a weak year; the method for wear and tear or inventory changes; past years’ numbers keep getting corrected.
The report is late or the auditor is suddenly changed; or profit on paper is high but dividends are low and borrowing is rising.
A student who suddenly corrects everyone’s marks themselves at the end of term has a suspicious report card.
Seven signs of dressed-up profit
ROIC says how much operating profit (after tax) the company makes each year for every 100 tomans tied up in its business.
Money tied up = machines + money owed by customers + inventory − money owed to suppliers.
In Iran machines are recorded at old prices, so this number is higher than reality; read it over 5 years and next to peers.
Growth only creates value when new money earns more than it costs. In the table, Company A made 18 tomans of profit with every new 100 tomans, and Company B only 4.
If you put 100 million into a dry cleaner’s and it makes 20 million a year, its return on capital is 20%. If the loan for that money costs 30% interest, growing it is a loss.
How much profit does each 100 tomans of capital make?
A competitive advantage means something a rival can’t easily copy.
Lower costs (for example its own mine), a brand and distribution network, a licence or scarce capacity like a port, or customers finding it hard to switch.
There are also policy advantages: cheap government feedstock, a preferential exchange rate or tariffs. But these go with one government decision.
A bakery that is the only bakery in the area has an advantage; but if the city gives a licence for a second bakery, that advantage is over.
Don’t assume an advantage the government gave is permanent; work out what happens if it goes.
A real advantage: profit per unit of sales has been low-swing for 5 years and return on capital higher than peers in most years.
High profit only in the year the dollar jumped isn’t an advantage; it’s a phase and it ends.
A restaurant that’s only busy on New Year’s Eve has no loyal customers; one that’s been busy every night for five years does.
Add up the cash the company made in 5 years and see where it went: repairs and renewal, new projects, dividends, paying off debt, or buying shares in other companies.
Did earlier projects finish on time and on budget? Did the promised profit arrive?
Does the dividend it pays fit the company’s needs or the main owner’s needs?
Is the company’s money sitting with the parent company?
If you want to know how well a family spends money, you look at where several years of income went: the house, the children’s education, or careless shopping.
Judge management from Codal:
Were its forecasts in past years cautious and did they come true? Has the CEO stayed for years, or do they keep changing?
Is the main owner aligned with small shareholders, or does it have many deals with the company?
Are reports on time and complete? Are small shareholders’ dividends paid on time?
Before giving a job to a builder, you look at their past work: did they finish on time? Were they fair to small customers too?
Judge management from Codal

Give 8 topics a score from 0 to 2: return on capital, return on new money, steadiness of profit per unit of sales, the ratio of cash to profit, the type of advantage, debt, project record, and report and audit quality.
12 to 16 means high quality; 8 to 11 medium; below 8 only if very cheap, with caution.
This score isn’t a buy signal; it tells you how far to trust the valuation number and how big a discount to ask for.
Like scoring a used car: engine, body, papers, accident history. A high score means you worry less, not that you pay any price.
